why: It gives a castle town's dyers' ward standing on water led from the castle moat, the siting our capital's dye works copy. Its limit is that it gives no founding date.

It gives the order of one Chinese temple's axis with its bell and drum towers, as rebuilt under the Ming (1428) and Qing (1720, 1747), the era our setting models. The axis and the site area cite nothing, and its one reference, a Haidian district chronicle, is cited only for events of 1986 and 1992. It is an imperially sponsored temple with a Qing travel palace on its south side, and a hillside temple outside the city, not a town temple. It faces east, which the article puts down to the Khitan custom of its Liao founding, where most Chinese temples face south, so the order of its halls is the usual one but the direction of its axis is not, and the article's site area of 6,000 m² disagrees with the far larger figure the Beijing cultural heritage bureau is reported to give, which could not be read.

It says what the building is and where it stood in the plan. It gives no sizes and says nothing of how many temples kept one. Its account of the plan rests on one 1986 general handbook (Mae Hisao, Kokenchiku no kiso chishiki), and its examples are great temples such as Hōryū-ji and Tōdai-ji, not the small temple of a village or town. Its short section on China covers palace and city bell towers, not temple ones.

It gives the range of heights of real premodern five-story pagodas that still stand outdoors, from about 16 m (Murō-ji) to about 55 m (Tō-ji, 1644); the miniature pagodas kept indoors and the modern concrete ones on the same page are not evidence for this. Heights carry no citations. It covers Japan only: the article itself says few wooden pagodas survive in China or Korea, and China's pagodas were often masonry and could be climbed. It lists only the pagodas that survived, and taller ones burned (it gives Gangō-ji's lost pagoda as about 73 m, uncited), so the top of the range understates the tallest ever built. Every pagoda on the list stands at a great or famous temple, and the list says nothing of how common pagodas were.

It gives the usual bearing of a Chinese town's non-temple pagoda: most often the southeast (xun), with east-northeast, south-southeast and south-southwest also allowed. Such a pagoda often stood at the water-mouth where the stream leaves the settlement, and local terrain and water flow bent the rule in practice. It is a short unsigned encyclopedia article (last revised 2020) resting on two modern books, chiefly Chen Zhihua's 2007 study of educational architecture. Its four bearings are what a Qing-dynasty geomantic manual, the Xiangzhai jingzuan, prescribes, not a count of where such pagodas actually stood, and only a handful of examples illustrate them. It describes mainly southern China and Vietnam, says such pagodas were fewer in the north and rarer still in the northeast and northwest, gives no era for the practice, and names nothing like it in Japan. It gives about three metres for a small stone brush-shaped marker, but no pagoda heights and no count of towns that built one.

It gives the Japanese case of a pagoda required by rule in every province: the edicts of 740 and 741 ordered a seven-story pagoda in each province, and the page says the kokubunji stood in or near the provincial capital and were, with the provincial office, the largest buildings of the province. It is not the only such case: the page names Chinese precedents in the state temples of the Sui and Tang, and Emperor Wen of Sui had relic pagodas built in more than a hundred prefectures in 601-604, which this page does not describe. Its own citations (the Shoku Nihongi and the Ruiju Sandai Kyaku, through a Kokubunji city museum sheet) carry the edict. The order is of the eighth century and held while the state paid for the temples: the page says most kokubunji decayed once that support ended and some survived as temples of other sects, and it says nothing of whether they kept their pagodas.

It states that management of division passed to leading farmers and village organizations in the medieval period, that rotation rules (bansui) fixed channel widths and gate-opening times by locality, and that the upstream-downstream quarrel was the standing one - the frame for how a ditch was split between villages. It is a short article without footnotes, so it carries the general pattern and no single village's practice.
It gives the size of an Edo kiln quarter in households, which is what makes a kiln a quarter rather than a shop on our capital. It attributes to a period source.

It describes, step by step, how two quarreling villages set their split each spring - measuring sticks cut to the length of two sealed vines, and water mouths built of sandbags to those lengths at a pool on the channel - which is a village-built division work with no permanent structure. It is one mountain canal as its present managers tell its history, with no dates for when the custom began.

It is the Edo-period precedent for a built structure at a split: a flume dividing one canal four ways in proportion to each district's cultivated area, which did not end the disputes. Its Edo-period section cites no source, so it carries the flume's existence and purpose and nothing more. Every number on the page (the 16 m diameter, the four arc ratios) is the 1941 concrete cylinder's, not the flume's. It says nothing of the flume's size or form, and nothing of it survives. The Kawasaki Board of Education's page on the site (https://www.city.kawasaki.jp/880/page/0000000312.html) is a closer source for the form: wooden gates, with inlet widths and downstream spreads set in proportion to irrigated area.

It describes a Chinese built division work: under the pavilion iron pillars part ten openings, three to the south county and seven to the north, and a stele records the split with a diagram. It gives no date for the pillars, and the split is between two counties, far above a village ditch.

It gives the dates (made in the 1660s, spread through the provinces by 1751-1780) and the one-person wheel's three sizes, 4.5, 5 and 5.5 shaku (the article says only "dimensions", not which one; reading them as the wheel's diameter is ours). The article has been flagged for missing sources since February 2015, its paragraph on sizes and prices has no footnote and calls the manual 農業便利論 instead of 農具便利論, so it carries the manual's 1822 Kansai figures at second hand. The manual itself is scanned publicly and is the source to read for a number.

It says the device came from China, was trodden by two people facing each other, was used mainly around the Kinki region in the early Edo period, and was driven out by the treadle wheel. A stub whose "Kinki, early Edo" claim rests on one footnote to a 2017 popular reference (Heibonsha's 日本史モノ事典), the rest on a 1977 annotated edition of Ōkura Nagatsune's 農具便利論 (1822). It records that its sources disagree on how widely the device spread. Ōkura says it was in general use in every province before the treadle wheel; Aoki Kunio says it broke easily and never spread widely. So it carries the device's form and the order in which the treadle wheel replaced it, not how common the chain pump was.

It says the pump spread further in the Song, suits the plains, and lifts water about 1 to 2 meters from a river or canal to fields by human or animal power - the Chinese counterpart of the Japanese devices, in the Song period the setting draws on. It is an article (last revised 2023) resting partly on popular web sources. The 1 to 2 meter lift is cited only to a modern popular-science page (Tongji University's school of mechanical engineering, for the China Digital Science and Technology Museum), and the article itself says the wooden pump was still worked in remote Chinese villages until pumps replaced it within living memory - so the figure describes an old form from modern observation, not a period record; the sentence on its spread in the Song carries no citation at all. The article also says (citing Elvin 1973) that the same pump reached Japan in the medieval period and was in common use among Kinai farmers by the Edo period.
It shows the Kyoto kilns clustered on the city's eastern side, the pattern our capital's works district follows, and it also shows some scattered, which keeps this page from saying never.

It defines the washing places a reader would see - araiba on a channel, kawado on the river, each a footing for washing clothes and vegetables - and the boards slotted into a channel to pond water for washing or split the flow, and the three-tier spring tank used top to bottom from drinking to muddy vegetables. It surveys one town; the facilities are old in form but the paper does not date each one.

It says that nearly every riverside house had a small landing at its door where clothes, vegetables and rice were washed and boats moored - the Jiangnan form of the washing place, one per house rather than one per village. That form belongs to the canal country of the lower Yangtze, where houses open straight onto the water; it is not the form for all of China, and a map of a drier region should not take one landing per house from it. It is a firm's blog, with no author, no date and no sources, so it is weak evidence for a date.
unsettled: The page is undated and describes the water towns as they survive, so the date of the landing form is not settled by it.

why: It says that in the dense canal country washing, shopping and cooking were all done at the riverside, and that the ideal house had one door on the street and one on the water. Only a teaser is readable. It describes the houses of southern Jiangsu and Zhejiang. It says the riverside life goes back "since ancient times" (自古以来), but a popular magazine piece with no references cannot prove that, so it carries the practice and no detail or number.

It gives the one number a map needs - the mound stood some tens of centimeters to 3 m above the main house - and the regional names (mizuya on the Kiso rivers, dangura on the Yodo, mizukura on the Shinano), and what was stored on each floor. It dates no mizuka. The height rests on one town's website (Itakura, on the Tone). The sentence on what each floor held cites nothing and lists a chabudai, a table of the Meiji era and later, so the stores are those of the mizuka that survived into the twentieth century, not of an Edo-period one. The form is said to be common across Japan's flood-prone lowlands; the name mizuka belongs to the Arakawa and Tone basins.

It gives the order of defenses at the house: the plot raised on fill first, then, because that was not enough, a still higher mound inside the plot with the mizuya on it, ranging from a hut to a spare dwelling, every one of them formerly used as a store. It is a short government page on one region, the Kaizu lowland in Gifu. It names no period and gives no date for the mounds or the buildings, and it gives no heights or sizes. So it supports the order of the defenses, not their date or any figure.

It dates the device: devised from the Taisho era, the first built in 1914 in Gifu - which is what makes the round divider an anachronism on a premodern map. It is used for that date only. The date itself rests on the article's own references. It covers Japan only: it says when the device was invented there, not that nothing like it existed in premodern China. That no such device stood in premodern China is this project's reading, not the page's.

It is the one page read that says how many of a city's residents rented, and that the share differed widely by region, which is what sets a town's back tenements apart from a great city's. The figures are estimates quoted in short excerpts, not a survey the page shows; the regional shares are of all urban residents, not of laborers, and it does not say which towns were counted or when, nor whether the Edo and Osaka estimate counts the samurai quarters or only the townsmen's wards. It describes Japan only: it carries the tenant share for the setting's Japanese-modeled towns and says nothing about a Chinese-modeled town.

It says the Edo-period placement broker (口入屋) in the cities provided a lodging (人宿) for the work-seekers he stood guarantor for. That is all it carries for our use. It does not say the lodging was in the broker's own house, and it says this of the broker who placed servants in samurai households and processions, not of the labor supplier (人夫出し) or gang boss. So \"a labor boss's house is larger than a laborer's\" is this project's inference from it. It is weak: it is mostly about the modern trade, and its Edo passage cites nothing (its one footnote, a 1935 Osaka report, covers only Meiji and Taishō rules). It glosses the Edo lodging with a Meiji-era term (たこ部屋). It describes Edo and the castle towns, a larger place than a small town. It gives no size or plan for the lodging. A closer public source, linked from the article itself, is Yoshida Masashi's 2010 typology of Edo servant brokers (Ritsumeikan Hōgaku 333-334); read it before relying on this claim.

It shows that one street of a busy highway town mixed heights rather than keeping one. Its sentence on the mix of heights cites a 2010 guidebook. It describes the townscape preserved today rather than a dated Edo-period survey: most of Seki's houses were built from the late Edo period through Meiji, and only about half of the district's buildings are Edo or Meiji, the rest reaching into the prewar Showa era. So the mix includes rebuilding after the Edo period and is not a picture of an Edo street. It covers one town only, so it says nothing about the share of each height elsewhere.

It is a surviving road town whose houses were built close enough to need fire walls between them. Its description rests almost wholly on a 2002 road-guide book (日本の道100選) and tourism pages, so it carries the form and not how common it was. It describes one preserved town as it stands, with buildings of several periods including Meiji sericulture houses; its one dated picture of the fire walls is captioned as a Meiji house (after 1868), it gives no Edo date for them, and it does not say how many towns had them.

It is evidence that traditional Chinese houses stood close enough to need a fire wall between them. It is strongest for Huizhou in the south-east and its neighbors (Hubei, Hunan, Jiangxi). It gives no date, no town and no measure of how close the houses stood, and it speaks of traditional buildings and their lanes generally, not of towns in particular: Hui-style walls are best known from villages. Its own sentence on stopping fire rests on a 2018 Epoch Times culture-site feature, and the one on narrow lanes on a popular book, so the claim is a secondary summary at best. It does not speak for the north.

It gives the height of the shophouse of South China and Southeast Asia: two or three stories, with the shop below and the family above. It is a short encyclopedia article flagged since 2017 as needing expansion. The sentence we use cites two studies of Singapore (a 2006 Berkeley working paper on Niucheshui and a 1992 Singapore book on public space), not any South Chinese town. Most of what it shows is the colonial-era shophouses of Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong and Taiwan, of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, and it credits their narrow plan and five-foot arcade to colonial tax, structural and building rules. So it is late, southern and mostly Southeast Asian evidence for a premodern county town, good for the form of the building and not for a number.

It is the one page read that gives a Chinese county seat's shop frontage and height in figures. It describes the surviving Ming and Qing town of one unusually rich merchant county, so its five-bay shop is likely at the wide end. Its examples are the town's listed heritage shops: the Juquantang pharmacy is five bays wide and over 9 m deep, while the Dadeheng draft bank's street fronts are three bays wide and one bay deep. It does not say how many shops were smaller. The building style it describes is the regional one of central Shanxi and north China (the page says so), so for a county seat elsewhere in China it stands in and does not measure one.
It supplies the definition that ties a house's roof orientation to where its door is, so either orientation puts a town house's door on the street.

It says in plain words that the back-to-back tenement (munewari nagaya) was usually a one-story unit of nine shaku by two ken, and that the street-front row was roomier (rooms of eight and four mats) and held fairly well-off small traders, which the encyclopedia pages imply but do not state. It does not say every back tenement was one story: the other kind it names, the wari nagaya divided across the ridge, had a mezzanine loft reached by a ladder (梯子をかけた中二階), so the one-story point holds for the back-to-back kind only. It describes Edo only; it is used for these two plain points, each consistent with the encyclopedia entries.

It states that a castle town's river landings were its outer port, the arrangement this page draws for a capital on a river. It describes the same town as the company archive cited beside it, so the two are not independent corroboration, and the form is generalized to any river capital from one case.

It states that a headman, though a peasant, could build a gate and a formal entrance step and did the village's business at home, where the other officials met - the privileges and the office work behind the headman's homestead on our maps. Its limits: no regional count of how many headmen used the right to a gate; and the page mixes the Edo headman with the medieval myoshu, so a passage must be read against its headword.

It is our evidence that dependent households lived in gate-huts and huts inside a larger farm's enclosure, counted with the master's household as one hearth. Its limits: the arrangement strongest early in it and, where it lasted the whole period, found mostly in mountain villages (the Heibonsha excerpt names those on the east bank of the Tenryu); the one-hearth counting is that of the register of houses, people and horses kept for corvée, not of every count (the temple registers appended the dependents to the master's entry); the hut-and-enclosure passage is a cut excerpt from the old edition of the Heibonsha encyclopedia; they give no size for the huts and no count of how many plots held them.

It defines the landless households whose housing the record asks about: not full villagers, with no part in village government, living by tenancy, labor or a craft. Its limits: they say nothing of where in the village the landless lived or how big their houses were.

It distinguishes the ordinary tenant, who rented fields, from the nago, who rented the house plot and house as well - which is why some poor households had no house of their own. Its limits:  the nago's standing changes. The house-renting distinction is Abiko's account of the stage from the mid-Edo period on, after the lords' policies to free the nago had weakened their bondage. It runs into the twentieth century, when nago survived mostly in backward and mountain districts (the former Morioka domain's system lasted until the postwar land reform). Before that stage, the unfree nago lived within the master's household and was not counted as a household of its own. The entries give no house size or siting.

It says a village meeting was often held at a village official's house, though temple halls and, in some regions, buildings in a shrine's or temple's grounds were used too, and that in the Kinki region villages set up meeting halls, often inside the tutelary shrine's precinct. Its limits: a folklorist's undated summary whose hosts include the ward head (区長), a post from the Meiji period onward, so what it describes reaches past the Edo period into modern village practice; it gives no dates for the Kinki halls beyond "from early times", no size for them and no count of how many villages had one; the rest of the page is about meetings that are not a village's.

It gives a rich farming family's compound in figures - about 2,300 tsubo of plot, a gatehouse, four storehouses and granaries - and a kin group's houses walled side by side, the top of the range a headman's or rich farmer's homestead reaches. Its limits: the family was a grand headman over 6,700 koku, a landlord and the largest grower of safflower in the whole Murayama region, far above a village headman; the buildings are of several dates, the branch's main house from 1920-1922; the 2,300 tsubo is the site inside and outside the residence (邸内・外), not the walled compound alone, and the page dates none of the main house's buildings, so the figures are the compound as it stands, not as it stood in the Edo period.

It lists what one headman's homestead held - main house with entrance and kitchen wings, two storehouses, a front gate, a gatehouse and an earthen wall - on a stated plot, which is what a headman's or rich farmer's homestead is drawn from. Its limits: one family in the Kinki region whose village was assessed at 1,600 koku, well above an ordinary village; and it lists the buildings without their sizes or arrangement.

It defines the rich farmer of the question - a village landlord of the mid-eighteenth century on, out of older landlords or out of trade - so the record can say who such a homestead belonged to. Its limits: Sasaki's definition belongs to one school of economic history, and the Britannica entry on the same page says the gōnō's nature is disputed. The class runs from the mid-eighteenth century into early Meiji, so traits the page gives for Bakumatsu and Meiji (new seed stock and new-style implements, silk-reeling ventures, 5-10 chō farms worked by hired labor) are later than the setting. It says nothing about houses, plots or buildings, and it describes Tokugawa Japan's later commercial economy rather than any one village.

It places the ancestral halls at the front of the village facing the pond, with the drying floor between, and says most Cantonese villages' halls stand so, and it records that some villages had no hall - which is where the map puts a hall and whether it draws one. Its limits: an article by two architecture lecturers, abridged in the repost, describing villages from fieldwork and maps, and dating no hall's placement to a period; the villages with no hall come from Feng Jiang's three layouts, cited at second hand from Feng Jiang's 2010 dissertation, which puts them in time order and is the closer source for when they stood; one region's form, the water country of the Cantonese delta (which the article says departs from the regular comb plan of Cantonese villages on hills and terraces), not south China at large.

It counts the halls and says those built in the city's second great period of hall building were mostly small and middling halls three bays wide and three halls deep, which confirms the common size. Its limits: its count of about 1,300 is credited only to unnamed scholars. The count is of halls of every size that survive today, not how many stood at any one time, and it covers a whole modern city, town and country together. Its size statement is for the new halls of one period, the Qing, not all of them.

It says a hall served for a lineage's meetings and feasts as well as its rites, that commoners were widely allowed to build them only from the Ming's Jiajing reign, and that more survive in the south than the north - where a south-China village's lineage met. Its limits: the meeting-and-feasting line rests on a lineage's own website and the Jiajing date on an anonymous web page; the southern survival has no citation and describes which halls outlasted the Cultural Revolution's destruction in the north, a modern survival pattern, not where halls were built before modern times, so it does not show that a south-China village had one; it gives no size or siting for a hall.

It gives one medieval village - Sugaura on Lake Biwa, about 70 households with three temples and twelve hermitages and cloisters in the fifteenth century, the count given without its source - and the author's view that temples probably came to many villages as the self-governing village formed. Its limits: it states the spread of village temples as a supposition ("it is thought"), not a finding. Sugaura, in Ōmi near the capital where self-governing villages were strongest, is a famous and well-documented exception rather than a typical village, and it stands in here for villages in general and for Kasuga in Kyushu, which the essay is about. Only three of its fifteen were temples; the twelve hermitages and cloisters housed monks who, the essay says, lived as villagers, supported themselves and fought beside them, not endowed temples. The figures are fifteenth-century, before the Edo parish system.
It shows that the landing was a place of business run by its wholesalers rather than a public quay, which is how this page describes it.

It gives a rate - about one hall for every twenty to thirty households, kept by the settlement - and a form and size, four posts under a tiled roof over a floor of about two mats, which is the only per-household count of wayside shrines read. Its limits: the tiled roof is the halls' form today, and it cites histories saying many were once thatched; the form and the rate are both regional, concentrated in Bingo and southern Bitchū and rare elsewhere, as the article itself says (a gazetteer of 1809 already called them rare in other provinces), so one hall for every twenty to thirty households is the density of the one district where these halls were thickest, not a general Japanese rate; the article takes that rate from a prefectural culture encyclopedia and gives no survey or year behind it; and the halls began as rest-houses for travelers that later took in jizo, so they are a wayside shrine by adoption.

It names the places a stone jizo stands - village boundaries, passes, crossroads, the foot of a bridge, graveyards - and says that in the Kinki region a jizo is kept for each town block, which is the town's count. Its limits: the block-by-block jizo is a Kinki custom, described as it is kept today rather than dated; and it gives no figure for how many a village kept.

It qualifies the block-by-block count - in Kyoto a block with no jizo of its own borrows one from a temple or hangs a painted one for the festival - and reports it "said" that from the Kantō eastward the dōsojin did the street jizo's work, which is why Jizō-bon never spread east. Its limits: no counts and no date for when the custom arose; the borrowing is a Kyoto observation, cited to a Kyoto City page; the eastern point is a hedged explanation of the festival's spread, cited to a town's report (Sekigahara), names the Kantō and the east rather than everything east of the Kinki (parts of Chūbu keep Jizō-bon), and does not say the east has no street jizo - so it lets an eastern map show a dōsojin, not leave the jizo out.

It records the Edo saying that Inari shrines were among the three things one met everywhere in the city, which is the one statement read on how thick small street shrines stood in a Japanese town. Its limits: the saying rests on one footnote to a 2009 popular guide to Inari (中村陽, supervising ed., イチから知りたい日本の神さま2 稲荷大神), not on period records; a saying is not a count; it is about Edo, the largest city in the country, rather than a county town; and by the article's own account Inari shrines grew thickest in eastern Japan because the cult was an Edo fashion, so it overstates what a town in western Japan, or one on the Chinese model, would have had. The same article gives a smaller place's figure: six Inari shrines in early-Meiji Musashi Fuchū, a post town, and 566 household shrines (屋敷神) counted across the modern city in a 1982 local-history survey. Those are household shrines over a modern city's area, not street shrines.

It is a witness from a farming district - Shin Buddhist by inference from the series' Kaga setting, which the page itself does not state - that a hamlet kept and ran its own cremation ground, the sanmai, and burned its own dead there until the ground closed in 1977, and it quotes a published scholar that, until cremation became universal after the Second World War, cremation as a custom had been confined to the Shin regions of Hokuriku and to Hiroshima and Yamaguchi. Its limits: one hamlet, remembered rather than surveyed, and the page itself does not name it or its province; the scholarly passage is quoted second-hand; and it gives no size, distance or siting for the ground. What it witnesses is the practice's twentieth-century survival, the ground's last use in 1977 within its speakers' memory, not its Edo-period form, and it does not date the ground's founding. And the quoted claim goes further than the national figures: in 1896 cremation was 26.8% of Japanese burials and over 65% in eight prefectures, among them Tokyo, Osaka, Niigata and Hokkaido as well as the Hokuriku three and Hiroshima, and the great cities cremated too; so the page supports cremation as the custom of the Shin regions, not as confined to them.

It says what stood at a local cremation ground - six jizo, which it says were always set there - which is what a map may draw beside the fire bed. Its limits: its "always" is the page's own generalization; it never dates when the ground was in use, so it cannot show that the six jizo stood there before the modern era rather than in the Meiji-to-Shōwa village practice from before municipal crematoria; it gives no size; and its only siting is general and unsourced: six jizo were set "at the entrance of graveyards" (a graveyard, not specifically a cremation ground).

In passing it places a small dragon-god shrine (a 祠) beside a named well, the Binsui-ire, at Mikura-hana, where the people of Amasegawa kept a festival on 20 November, which is a readable instance of a small shrine at a well. Its limits: this passage repeats a twentieth-century folklore study (Takaya Shigeo, 雨の神, 1984), so the festival is as that study recorded it, not a present-day observation; the shrine's founding date is not given, so nothing here shows it is premodern; it is one shrine, mentioned in a legend article rather than a survey; and it is a water-deity shrine tied to rain-prayer rather than a wayside one.

It names the cargo-specialized landings of one Edo river, the pattern our wharf district's specialized quays follow. It is Edo, the largest city in the country, whose quay specialization a provincial seat would not match.

A signed entry (Katō Hideaki) in a modern general encyclopedia. Its sentence on enclosure is worded generally, but it follows directly on the list of Edo's six great notice-board sites and its 35 others, so it may describe the shogun's capital and its major sites rather than a village's or a small town's board; none of the other dictionaries on the page mentions an enclosure at all. It names the enclosures - a palisade, a stone wall, a turf bank - as alternatives without saying which was usual or giving any size.

It records one board's original seat - at the crossroads with the Hida road, a short way up the slope from where the reconstruction stands - and the reason given, that more people would see it there. One post town; it gives no date for the siting and no source for the reason.

A modern Japanese encyclopedia's entry (Heibonsha's Sekai Daihyakka Jiten; Kotobank shows only an excerpt, with no author's name) naming the roadside communal well as a recognized kind with its own word. It is one sentence, about Japanese wayside facilities in general; the sentence itself carries no date, and the customs cited beside it are Edo-period Kyoto (the 1670s to the 1700s), so it bears on pre-Meiji Japan and says nothing of China. It says nothing of how common such wells were, how they were built, or whether villages had them.

A signed encyclopedia entry covering Japan in general and the period before the hand pump, which is the period the maps draw. It names the forms without saying where or when each prevailed, cites no period record, and gives no dimensions. The bucket well lasted until the hand pump and piped water, which is modern, so the forms it describes were probably recorded by folklorists in the late nineteenth and twentieth centuries; that they are Edo or older is our inference, not the entry's statement. It speaks for Japan only; for the Chinese side of the setting it is an analog.
